title: Bitrise Build Hub vs GitHub-Hosted Runners
description: Bitrise Build Hub runs your GitHub Actions jobs on M4 Macs and AMD Linux machines. Compare it with GitHub-hosted runners on price per minute, macOS hardware, concurrency, images, caching and billing, and see which jobs are worth moving.
introduction:
This is not a choice between two CI systems. Bitrise Build Hub keeps GitHub Actions as the orchestrator. Your workflows, triggers, secrets and logs stay on GitHub. Build Hub only supplies the machines: you install a GitHub App, create a machine pool, and change runs-on for the jobs you want to move. So the real question is where each job should run.

The answer depends mostly on the operating system. On macOS, the gap is large. GitHub's standard macOS runner is a 3 vCPU M1 with 7 GB of RAM at $0.062 a minute, and its biggest Apple silicon runner is a 5 vCPU M2 Pro at $0.102. Build Hub's smallest Mac is a 5 vCPU M4 with 14 GB at $0.03 a minute from the plan budget. Per vCPU, that is under a third of GitHub's price, on newer hardware.

We measured this on a real app. Over 17 runs, the Wikipedia iOS app's build and unit tests took a median 5.6 minutes per job on a Build Hub M4 Large and 15.4 minutes on GitHub's standard macOS runner, 2.7 times faster. Billed per started minute at list price, with Build Hub's machine start-up counted, that is $0.21 against $0.99 a run, about a fifth of the cost.

On Linux, the prices are close. Build Hub charges $0.003125 per vCPU minute on every self-serve size, and GitHub charges about $0.003 for its x64 runners and less for arm64. Build Hub's smallest Linux machine has 4 vCPU, so a short lint job costs more there than on a 2-core GitHub runner. Linux jobs only get cheaper on Build Hub if they finish much faster, and that depends on the job. On the Thunderbird Android app, the 16 vCPU Linux XLarge ran the build and the unit tests about twice as fast as GitHub's 4 vCPU runner. It costs four times as much per minute, so each Linux job cost about twice as much: on Linux, what you buy is time.

For a mobile team, the two results add up. We ran one pull request pipeline, the iOS build and tests plus the Android build and the Android tests, started together. With a Linux pool that can run two machines at once, it finished in a median 18.5 minutes on Build Hub over seven runs, against 43.6 minutes on GitHub over 17 runs. At list price a run cost about the same: a median $1.77 on Build Hub against $1.79 on GitHub, over 17 runs each, and the ranges overlap. The Macs save money and the 16 vCPU Linux machines cost more per minute, so the two roughly cancel out. Set the pool maximum to at least the number of Linux jobs that start together. In our first ten runs the Linux pool maximum was 1, so the second Android job waited a median 15 minutes for the first, and the pipeline took a median 35 minutes. Part of the later drop came from faster Android builds, not only from the setting.

The billing models also differ. GitHub bills each job per minute, rounded up, against included minutes. Build Hub sells a monthly tier, and the tier fee becomes your compute budget. Build Hub bills per started minute, and the billed time includes the machine's start-up. The tier also sets how many Macs can run at the same time.

This page compares the two on hardware, price, concurrency, images, caching, security and setup. Prices are list prices from each vendor's pricing page, checked on 18 October 2026. Bitrise provided the Build Hub workspace for our tests, and the workflows and every run are public in the benchmark repository.

toolA.name: Bitrise Build Hub
toolA.description: Managed runners for GitHub Actions from Bitrise, the mobile CI company. M4 Macs and AMD EPYC Linux machines register with GitHub as self-hosted runners, so workflows stay on GitHub and only the runs-on label changes. Sold as monthly tiers whose fee becomes a shared macOS and Linux compute budget.
pros: M4 Macs from $0.03 a minute (5 vCPU, 14 GB), under a third of GitHub's macOS price per vCPU
Up to 10 vCPU and 28 GB of RAM per Mac on self-serve plans, against 5 vCPU and 14 GB on GitHub
Workflows stay in GitHub Actions: switching a job is a runs-on change after the GitHub App and machine pool are set up
Mobile build stacks with Xcode, Android SDK, Flutter and React Native, and Bitrise states that new Xcode versions arrive within 24 hours of release
A co-located GitHub Actions cache backend with 100 GB per workspace on every tier, plus an optional remote build cache for Gradle, Bazel and Xcode
Ephemeral VMs, SOC 2 Type II, US or EU region locking, and SSH or VNC access to a running job
One budget covers both macOS and Linux jobs
cons: Linux costs about the same per vCPU as GitHub
The smallest Linux machine is 4 vCPU, so light jobs cost more than on a 1 or 2-core GitHub runner
No Windows, no Linux arm64 and no GPU machines
When the monthly budget is used up, jobs stop running on Build Hub unless you turn on pay-as-you-go, which costs twice the standard rate per minute
Low tiers cap how many Macs run at once (2 M4 Large machines on Basic Tier 1)
Bitrise stacks are not GitHub's runner images, so jobs that rely on preinstalled tools may need setup steps
M4 Pro and M5 Pro Macs are only on the Enterprise plan

toolB.name: GitHub-Hosted Runners
toolB.description: The runners GitHub provides for GitHub Actions: Linux, Windows and macOS, x64 and arm64, from 1-core containers to 96-core larger runners and GPU machines. Billed per job minute, rounded up, with included minutes on every plan and free standard runners for public repositories.
pros: Nothing to set up: runs-on: ubuntu-latest works in every repository
Free standard runners for public repositories, and 2,000 to 50,000 included minutes a month by plan
Every operating system and architecture, including Windows, arm64 and GPU runners
Small and cheap options for light jobs, such as ubuntu-slim at $0.002 a minute
The actions/runner-images images are the reference that most actions and examples assume
Pay-as-you-go billing with no prepaid budget to run out
cons: macOS is expensive: $0.062 a minute for a 3 vCPU M1, about 10 times the Linux rate
The largest Apple silicon runner is a 5 vCPU M2 Pro with 14 GB of RAM
Every job is rounded up to a whole minute, which adds up across matrix builds
Free, Pro and Team plans run at most 5 macOS jobs at the same time
Included minutes do not apply to larger runners
The free cache is 10 GB per repository, and entries not used for 7 days are evicted

useCases.scenario: An iOS team spends most of its Actions bill on macOS minutes
useCases.explanation: This is where Build Hub is clearly cheaper. A 5 vCPU M4 at $0.03 a minute replaces a 3 vCPU M1 at $0.062 or a 5 vCPU M2 Pro at $0.102. In our test of the Wikipedia iOS app, one build and test job took a median 5.6 minutes on the M4 Large and 15.4 minutes on GitHub's M1 over 17 runs, so each run cost $0.21 instead of $0.99. In separate runs, the M4 XLarge was only about 10% faster than the M4 Large on this app, so start with the M4 Large. On the Enterprise plan, the M4 Pro XLarge took 23% less time than the M4 Large in the same separate runs (3 each), at a flat price instead of a per-minute rate. Check that the tier you pick has enough macOS concurrency for your busiest hour.

useCases.scenario: A mobile team builds Android and iOS from the same repository
useCases.explanation: One Build Hub budget pays for both the Macs and the Linux machines, and the stacks come with the Android SDK, Xcode, Flutter and React Native. In our test, a pipeline with the Wikipedia iOS build and tests plus the Thunderbird Android build and tests, started together, finished in a median 18.5 minutes on Build Hub (M4 Large and Linux XLarge) against 43.6 minutes on GitHub's standard runners. At list price a run cost about the same, a median $1.77 against $1.79. Set the Linux pool maximum to at least 2: with a maximum of 1, the two Android jobs ran one after the other and the pipeline took a median 35 minutes. The Macs save money and the Linux machine saves time. Keep short Linux jobs, such as linting, on GitHub's small runners, where they cost less.

useCases.scenario: A backend team runs only Linux jobs: tests, Docker builds and linters
useCases.explanation: Build Hub's Linux price per vCPU is about the same as GitHub's, and its smallest machine has 4 vCPU. Unless your heavy jobs finish much faster on Build Hub's AMD EPYC machines, you will not save money. Measure a few heavy jobs on both before you move them.

useCases.scenario: An open source project with public repositories
useCases.explanation: Standard GitHub-hosted runners are free for public repositories, including 4 vCPU Linux machines and macOS. A paid runner only makes sense if a specific job, such as a large iOS build, is too slow.

useCases.scenario: A team that also builds and tests on Windows
useCases.explanation: Build Hub has no Windows machines. You can still move macOS jobs to Build Hub and keep Windows jobs on GitHub, because runs-on is set per job.

useCases.scenario: A company that needs builds to run in the EU, with SOC 2 evidence from the runner vendor
useCases.explanation: Build Hub can lock jobs to US or EU data centers and has a SOC 2 Type II report. GitHub-hosted runners are covered by GitHub's own compliance reports, and larger runners with Azure private networking run in the region of your subnet. Check which jobs and data each option covers before you decide.

faqs.question: Do I have to leave GitHub Actions to use Build Hub?
faqs.answer: No. Build Hub machines register with GitHub as self-hosted runners. Your workflow files, triggers, secrets and logs stay on GitHub. After you install the GitHub App and create a machine pool, you move a job by changing its runs-on label, and you can move it back the same way.

faqs.question: Is Build Hub cheaper than GitHub-hosted runners?
faqs.answer: On macOS, yes, by a wide margin at list price: $0.03 a minute for a 5 vCPU M4, against $0.062 for GitHub's 3 vCPU M1 and $0.102 for its 5 vCPU M2 Pro. On Linux, the price per vCPU is about the same as GitHub's. Remember that you pay the tier fee every month, whether or not you use the whole budget.

faqs.question: What happens when the Build Hub budget runs out?
faqs.answer: By default, your GitHub Actions jobs stop running on Build Hub runners until the next monthly cycle. You can turn on pay-as-you-go to keep them running after the budget is used up. Its per-minute rate is twice the standard rate for the machine type, so a higher tier can cost less if you run out regularly. You can cap pay-as-you-go spend from $5 up to unlimited, and Bitrise stops starting runners for your jobs at the cap.

faqs.question: Are Build Hub images the same as GitHub's runner images?
faqs.answer: No. Build Hub uses Bitrise stacks, not actions/runner-images. Most mobile tooling is preinstalled, and bitrise.io/stacks lists what each macOS and Linux stack includes. A job that expects a tool from GitHub's image may need a setup action first: our Android UI tests needed four OpenGL and X11 packages on the Linux stack. Run your workflows on a test pool before you switch a busy branch.

faqs.question: Is Build Hub faster than GitHub-hosted runners?
faqs.answer: For iOS, yes. We ran the Wikipedia iOS app's build and unit tests at a pinned commit, 17 times on each side. The job took a median 337 seconds on a Build Hub M4 Large (5 vCPU) and 922 seconds on GitHub's standard M1 runner (3 vCPU), so it was 2.7 times faster. We did not test GitHub's 5 vCPU M2 Pro runner, which costs $0.102 a minute. In separate runs, the M4 Pro XLarge, which is on the Enterprise plan only, took a median 250 seconds over 3 runs, about 23% less time than the M4 Large's 323 seconds in the same separate runs. Enterprise is sold at a flat price limited by concurrency, not per minute, so it has no per-run price to compare. For Android, the Thunderbird app's build job took a median 20.7 minutes on the 16 vCPU Linux XLarge against 43.4 minutes on GitHub's 4 vCPU runner, and its unit test job took 7.8 against 16.1 minutes.

faqs.question: Does GitHub charge for self-hosted runners such as Build Hub?
faqs.answer: Not today. GitHub announced a $0.002 per minute platform charge for self-hosted runners in December 2025, then postponed it. GitHub's docs say Actions usage is free on self-hosted runners. GitHub called it a postponement, not a cancellation, so check the current billing docs.

decisionMatrix.criteria: Most of your Actions bill is macOS minutes
You need more than 5 vCPU or 14 GB of RAM on a Mac without an Enterprise contract
Developers wait more than 20 minutes for an Android or iOS pipeline
You want SSH or VNC access to a running build
Your jobs run only on Linux
You build on Windows or need arm64 or GPU runners
You want zero setup and pure pay-as-you-go billing
You build Android and iOS apps from one pipeline

verdict.summary: Treat Build Hub as a place to send some of your GitHub Actions jobs, not as a full switch. For macOS it is the stronger choice: newer M4 hardware, up to 28 GB of RAM on self-serve plans, and in our test an iOS build and test job that ran 2.7 times faster for about a fifth of the price. For Linux, Build Hub's 16 vCPU machine finished our Android build and tests in about half the time, but GitHub's own runners cost less per job, have smaller sizes for light jobs, and cover Windows, arm64 and GPU. Because runs-on is set per job, the setup that saves the most is usually a mix: macOS on Build Hub, heavy Linux jobs on Build Hub when waiting time matters, and light Linux jobs on GitHub.
verdict.recommendation: Choose Bitrise Build Hub for iOS and other macOS jobs, and for mobile teams that build Android and iOS together. Keep GitHub-hosted runners for Linux, Windows and public repositories, and for light jobs where a 1 or 2-core runner is enough.
